construction.admit: Admit an envelope at (credential, n) iff: (1) it verifies, row 4; (2) n == held(c).seq + 1; (3) link_n is computed from the link the client itself holds, row 5; (4) a signed head at position >= n verifies against **that** link rather than the one it carries. Otherwise HOLD — the position or the head is not yet available — or REFUSE. A second link at a position already held needs no fifth condition: it arrives at or below the mark and condition 2 refuses it
construction.mint: Mint at own_held + 1, reserving the position in a transaction that stages the spool row with it (S0-4 return, FU-10). On a **definite refusal** at n — all five subject fields this envelope’s own, verified under the K_accept the lineage currently certifies — re-mint at the same n under the current epoch; row 4 forbids skipping. On no answer, wait. Re-minting a position that may have been accepted is self-equivocation, and the rule above refuses it permanently on every other device
construction.baseline: held(c) starts at the adopted checkpoint's head-vector entry for c, or at (0, 32 zero bytes). Replaying from a checkpoint and replaying from genesis are the same operation, which is what makes a checkpoint a retention floor
construction.heads_record: Row 3’s record format with kind = 'heads', in its own object store under the same store subkey, sharing the content store’s `seq` sequence. plaintext = LP("done/heads/v1") || head_vector, with row 7’s serialization verbatim
construction.write_order: The content batch commits first and the heads record after it. A crash between them re-delivers admitted positions, which is idempotent; the reverse order advances the mark past an operation that was never applied, and that operation is then below the baseline forever. Same direction as §6.1’s trim, for the same reason

retention.own_outbound_envelopes: Each device retains its own outbound envelopes back to the **second-newest** checkpoint it has seen admitted, not the newest. §11.3 test 8 falls back to the next-newest checkpoint and §14.3 re-envelops this device’s suffix from whichever checkpoint it applied; a device trimmed to the newest cannot supply that. Counting two locally needs no service field and no retention parameter on the wire
retention.suffix_beside_a_checkpoint: The durable store retains each retained checkpoint’s suffix from that checkpoint’s head vector forward. Row 7 retains at least two checkpoints, so it retains at least two suffixes
retention.local_head_vector: A high-water mark, not a log: one entry per credential, replaced in place. No depth, and no growth beyond the credential count

not_here.primitives: SHA-256, HKDF, AES-256-GCM and Ed25519 KATs are row 1’s, in test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json.
not_here.links: The link and head constructions are row 5’s and are audited in finalization.json.
not_here.serialization: The head-vector serialization and its digest are row 7’s.
not_here.envelope: The envelope whose digest each link binds is row 4’s.

k_accept.role: The service's hot acceptance-signing key (row 5), certified at epoch 9 — the certification in force. It signs heads and refusals and nothing else.

k_accept_retired.role: The acceptance key epoch 8 certified, rotated away at epoch 9 (an ordinary epoch event, §7.5). Genuinely certified once, currently certified nowhere — the delayed old-key compromise FU-06 closes signs with exactly this key.

refusal.why: §7.4 makes a definite refusal the only license to re-mint a position and requires it be authenticated. Nothing could express one: row 15's transition Outcome names a transition, not an envelope (S0-4, f-745e332-envelope-refusal-carrier-missing). K_accept signs it, because acceptance and refusal are two answers from one decision domain -- a separate refusal key would be an authority that can induce a re-mint without being able to accept anything, and a compromised K_accept can already forge heads.
refusal.message: Refuse = LP("done/position-refuse/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(credential_id) || LP(dec position) || LP(hex refused_digest) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(reason) || LP(hex parent_refusal), signed by K_accept. refusal_id = SHA-256(Refuse). epoch is the refused envelope’s own referenced epoch -- the fifth subject field (FU-06, the S0-4 return).
refusal.verification: The client resolves K_accept from the epoch in force in its authenticated lineage -- the same certification the acceptance heads resolve through -- never from the answer and never merely from an epoch it once held; then requires all five subject fields to be its own envelope's, the epoch included. A refusal under a retired epoch's key fails the signature; one naming another epoch fails the subject; both are silence (FU-06, A-03, the S0-4 return).
refusal.permanence: A refusal closes (workspace, credential, position, refused_digest, epoch) forever. A late resubmission is answered with the same Refuse message under the live K_accept: refusal_id binds the message and not the signature, so the licence survives an ordinary rotation. Without permanence a client could re-mint on a refusal and have its original accepted behind it -- two links at one position, which §7.5 reads as a compromised credential.
refusal.chain: A successor names the refusal_id that licensed it, and that refusal licenses its own position and no other -- a successor at n+1 under a refusal for n is the skipping row 4 forbids. The first attempt at a position names 32 zero bytes. A successor may itself be refused, and nothing caps the chain. Nothing caps the attempts either: RC-4A proposed a sole successor slot per refusal, and every attempt at a position competes for the one digest that position will ever accept, so at most one accepted digest per position already permits only one to win. Removing the slot from the executable model changed no result (S0-4).

lineage.note: The certification history the client holds (§13.5, ancestor-checked). The verifier is always certified[tip]; the history rows exist so a retired key is a value here rather than a description.

refusal.uncertified_key: RFC 8032 §7.1 TEST 3 -- a key no epoch certifies.
refusal.retired_epoch_key: KEYS.k_accept_retired -- certified at epoch 8, rotated away at 9. A-03’s delayed old-key compromise signs with exactly this key, and the resolution refuses it.

vectors.name: twelve-positions-and-a-baseline-at-nine
vectors.why: The phone's chain through a rotation between positions 9 and 10, checkpointed at 9. Replayed from genesis and replayed from the checkpoint's baseline it reaches the same link at position 12, which is the whole of why everything below a checkpoint may be dropped.

self_equivocation.why: The same credential at the same position with a different update, so that “a different link at a held position” is a value rather than a description. Nothing distinguishes this from an attacker holding the credential, which is why an honest client that re-mints without a definite refusal breaks its own chain permanently.

head_checked_against_its_carried_link.why: §7.5’s *must not happen*, shown succeeding. A client at a divergent position 11 computes a different link at 12; checking the head against the link the **head** carries admits it anyway, because that check is satisfied by the head being well-formed and says nothing about what the client replayed. The negative `numeric-mark-without-its-link` is the same inputs under the correct check.

local_rollback.why: An earlier heads record, genuinely sealed under the same subkey and the same AAD shape. It **opens**, and it is published here rather than in must_fail because it does: an AAD authenticates a record and cannot order two valid ones. The bound is in the selection document — a rollback is exploitable only in collusion with a service willing to sign a second link at a held position, which is the bound §7.5 already states for equivocation.

must_fail.name: position-does-not-follow
must_fail.mutate: Offer position 12 while the mark is at 10. Refused before any hashing. **Row 4 is what makes this a refusal rather than a policy**: `seq` is the credential’s own outbound position and its accepted position as one number, so a client computes every link itself and cannot be told where a chain got to.

must_fail.name: numeric-mark-without-its-link
must_fail.mutate: A mark whose *number* is 11 and whose *link* is position 10’s — a client that advanced a counter without keeping what it replayed. The position check passes and the computed link is wrong, so no signed head covers it. **This is the argument for the carrier’s shape**: §7.5 says a numeric high-water mark is not a finalization boundary, and one level down it is not an anti-replay state either.

must_fail.name: equivocated-position-below-the-mark
must_fail.mutate: The equivocated position 7 offered while the mark is at 12. Refused by the position check alone — which is why *no second link at a held position* needs no state of its own and the carrier can be a mark rather than a log.

must_fail.name: equivocated-position-at-the-mark
must_fail.mutate: The equivocated position 7 offered while the mark is at 6, so the position check passes and the link is computed honestly. It differs from the accepted one, and the service signed a head over the accepted one. **This is also the shape an honest client produces if it re-mints at a position it never learned was refused**, which is why the outbound rule waits rather than retries.

must_fail.name: baseline-from-another-checkpoint
must_fail.mutate: Replay positions 10 through 12 from a head vector that is not the adopted checkpoint’s. The links diverge from the first position onward, so a substituted baseline cannot be walked forward into agreement with a signed head.

must_fail.name: heads-record-read-as-state
must_fail.mutate: Open the heads record with `kind` claimed as `state`. **Row 3’s attack with a second victim**: a `state` record supersedes everything before it, so a heads record reinterpretable as one would be a way to make the trim delete content through its own path — and, here, to drop the anti-replay baseline while doing it.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-principal
must_fail.mutate: Open the heads record as though it belonged to another principal on the same profile.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Open it as though it belonged to another workspace.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-version
must_fail.mutate: Open it claiming another record format version.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-generation
must_fail.mutate: Open it claiming another content-key generation.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-seq
must_fail.mutate: Open it claiming another store sequence number. `seq` is shared with the content store rather than restarting here, so row 3’s per-generation nonce budget stays one comparison over one sequence.

must_fail.name: heads-aad-only-renumbered-label
must_fail.mutate: Open it under "done/store/v2".

must_fail.name: wrong-store-subkey
must_fail.mutate: Derive the store subkey for another workspace. The AAD half is `heads-aad-only-workspace`.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-label
must_fail.mutate: Renumber the message label to "done/position-refuse/v2".

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-version
must_fail.mutate: Claim v = 2.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-workspace
must_fail.mutate: A refusal minted for another workspace.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-credential
must_fail.mutate: Another credential's position.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-position
must_fail.mutate: Position 14 rather than 13.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-digest
must_fail.mutate: Another envelope digest. This is the field that makes the refusal permanent rather than a status, so it is the one an attacker would move.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-epoch
must_fail.mutate: Claim a later epoch.

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-reason
must_fail.mutate: "policy" rather than "stale-epoch".

must_fail.name: aad-only-refusal-parent
must_fail.mutate: Name a parent refusal that was never issued. Binding it is what makes a re-mint require a licence at all, and what stops a licence for position n being spent at n+1.

must_fail.name: refusal-for-another-position
must_fail.mutate: A validly signed refusal for position 14, presented to a client waiting at 13. It verifies, and it licenses nothing here.

must_fail.name: refusal-for-another-digest
must_fail.mutate: A validly signed refusal for a different digest at this position — the shape a service would produce for an attempt this client never made.

must_fail.name: refusal-for-another-credential
must_fail.mutate: A validly signed refusal for another credential's position 13.

must_fail.name: refusal-for-another-workspace
must_fail.mutate: A validly signed refusal for the same credential's position 13 in another workspace. The S0-9 follow-up found genuine workspace substitution un-isolated; this is the case (S0-4 return).

must_fail.name: refusal-for-another-epoch
must_fail.mutate: A validly signed refusal naming epoch 9 against the attempt that referenced epoch 8 — this envelope's other fields, another envelope's epoch. It verifies under the certification in force, and the fifth subject field is what refuses it (FU-06, S0-4 return).

must_fail.name: unsigned-error-body
must_fail.mutate: An error body with no signature, which §7.4 calls silence in as many words. The client resubmits the identical bytes from its spool rather than re-minting — and that is safe whichever unknown it was, because at most one digest is ever accepted at a position.

must_fail.name: refusal-under-an-uncertified-key
must_fail.mutate: The same refusal signed by a key no epoch certifies. Anything that can withhold an answer can manufacture one, which is why §7.4 requires the refusal be authenticated rather than merely definite.

must_fail.name: refusal-under-a-retired-epoch-key
must_fail.mutate: The same refusal — every subject field this envelope's own — signed by the key epoch 8 certified and the rotation at 9 retired. A perfect subject under a genuinely once-certified key licenses nothing, because the verifier resolves from the lineage's current certification and never from the answer. This is A-03's delayed old-key compromise, refused (FU-06, S0-4 return).
